# Shared-vocabulary scope-leak fixture

## What this is

Two corpus definitions for two different projects that share vocabulary, plus
the session membership each project resolves to. They are the input to the
leak test in `scope_test.go`, which asserts one property: a session scoped to
Project 1 never receives a Project 3 record while no relationship edge is
declared between the two scopes, and receives them only once such an edge is
declared.

The two projects deliberately hold near-identical record ids
(`.../docs/retrieval.md#scope-filter` and `#ranking` in both). Shared
vocabulary is what makes the test meaningful: if scope membership were
skipped, dropped, or applied after ranking instead of before it, a query from
either side would match the other side's records on content alone and the
leak would be invisible in any test whose corpora talk about different
subjects.

## Provenance

These are hand-written scenario inputs, not captured output. Nothing in them
was generated by the package under test, and the test authors no expected
bytes from this package's own output: it asserts a property (zero records
crossing the boundary, then exactly the declared ones crossing once an edge
exists), so there is no golden here that could silently record whatever the
implementation happens to do.

The scenario itself is fixed by the phase plan, which requires this specific
two-project shared-vocabulary case and requires it to be asserted in CI. The
shape of the corpus and record rows is the shape defined by `model.go` in the
package next to this directory; the field spellings are the JSON tags on
`Corpus`, `Record` and `Membership`, so a rename that breaks the model breaks
the fixture load rather than being papered over.

The scope ids follow the session scope model's composition (a user scope, a
workspace both projects sit under, and the project scope itself). They are
placeholders for real resolved ids on purpose: this package treats a scope
reference as opaque, and a fixture that embedded one machine's real resolved
ids would assert something about the resolver rather than about membership.

## Files

| File | Role |
| --- | --- |
| `corpus_project1.json` | Project 1's corpus, its records, and the membership a Project 1 session resolves to. Includes one record tagged `untrusted-source` inside an otherwise trusted corpus, so the propagation assertion has a real mixed corpus to run against rather than a uniform one. |
| `corpus_project3.json` | Project 3's corpus, its records, and its own session membership. Its corpus is `shared`, which is the widest class core grants: even at that class, no edge means no reach. |

## Why Project 3 is `shared` and not `scope-local`

A leak test whose far-side corpus is marked private proves very little, because
the narrow class alone would withhold the records. Marking Project 3 `shared`
means the only thing standing between a Project 1 session and Project 3's
records is the absent relationship edge. That is the control under test.
